chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf from Ali ibn Mahziyar from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Bazee' said:

Indeed, a man from our companions died without making a will, so his case was referred to the judge of Kufa, who appointed Abd al-Hamid ibn Salim as the guardian of his property. The deceased had left behind young heirs, movable goods, and female slaves. Abd al-Hamid sold the movable goods, but when he intended to sell the female slaves, his heart weakened regarding their sale, as the deceased had not appointed him specifically for this, and his guardianship was by the judge's order because they are 'furuj' (parts of the body/property). Muhammad said: I mentioned this to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said: 'May I be your ransom, a man from our companions dies and does not appoint anyone as executor, and leaves female slaves, so the judge appoints one of us to sell them or a man from us undertakes this, and his heart weakens because they are furuj. What do you think about that?' He said: 'If the guardian is like you and like Abd al-Hamid, there is no harm.' And so and so, and she began nodding her head saying 'Yes,' not speaking with words, so they both approved that for her.

From him, from Umar ibn Ali, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamadani, who said: I wrote to him: 'A man wrote a document containing what he intended to bequeath. Is it obligatory upon his heirs to carry out what is in the document by his own hand, even if he did not command them to do so?' He wrote back: 'If his children execute everything they find in their father's document in the manner of piety and otherwise.'

From him, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, who said: The slave of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan died and left a sister, and he bequeathed all his wealth to him (peace be upon him). He said: So we sold his movable goods and they amounted to one thousand dirhams, and it was brought to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him). I wrote to him and informed him that he had bequeathed all his wealth to him, so he took one-third of what I sent to him and returned the remainder, and ordered me to give it to his heir.

From him, from al-Abbas, from one of our companions, who said: I wrote to him: 'May I be your ransom, a woman bequeathed to a woman and gave her five hundred dirhams, and she had a husband and children. She ordered her to give a share from it to some of her daughters and to direct the remainder to the Imam.' He (peace be upon him) wrote back: 'Direct one-third of that to me, and the remainder is divided according to the shares of Allah (Exalted and Mighty) among the heirs.'

key_terms.إِجَاز: To approve or validate a legal action
key_terms.سَهْم: Share or portion, often referring to the Imam's share in bequests
key_terms.فُرُوج: Parts of the body; here used to refer to female slaves as property/asset
key_terms.قَيِّم: Guardian or trustee appointed to manage the estate

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a judge-appointed guardian selling property when the deceased did not specify the executor?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* elucidates the jurisprudential distinction between a testamentary executor and a judicially appointed guardian (*qayyim*), highlighting the Imam's reliance on the piety and discretion of trusted companions like Abd al-Hamid in managing estates of minors. It further clarifies the binding nature of written bequests even without explicit command and refines the distribution of specific gifts to the Imam versus general inheritance shares, reflecting the practical application of *wasiyyah* in early Shia legal practice. The text underscores the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence in adapting guardianship roles to the specific circumstances of the deceased's assets and heirs.
